Glucose to insulin, step by step

Press a step to light it, or let the tour walk through them. Each step shows the cell as it is at the end of that step.

Key glucose insulin Ca²⁺ K⁺ ATP ADP membrane charge (− at rest, + once activated)

Hover or focus any part for an explanation. Drag glucose low and the later steps weaken: the K-ATP channels stay open and no insulin is released.

Sources

Educational only, not medical advice. On a narrow screen, swipe the figure sideways to see every label and tap a step button to light it. Schematic, not to scale: levels come from a qualitative model, not measurements. Every level in the animation is qualitative; the only numbers are those quoted from the cited sources in the hover text.

  • Steps 2 to 5. Glucokinase as the rate-limiting glucose sensor; the cytoplasmic ATP/ADP ratio (not ATP alone) as the signal; Kir6.2 (KCNJ11) + SUR1 (ABCC8) K-ATP octamer, inhibited by ATP and stimulated by MgADP; depolarisation; L-type (CACNA1C/D), P/Q-type (CACNA1A) and T-type Ca²⁺ channels in human beta cells, with L-type dominant in mouse; SNARE-dependent exocytosis of docked dense-core granules, targeted towards the capillaries: Rorsman and Ashcroft, Physiol Rev 2018 (PMID 29212789; full text read, PMC5866358).
  • Step 1, transporter. Human beta cells express predominantly GLUT1, with lower GLUT2 (abstract read); rodent beta cells use mainly GLUT2: De Vos et al., J Clin Invest 1995 (PMID 7593639).

Notes. The transporter is shown as a generic glucose transporter: GLUT1 predominates in human beta cells and GLUT2 is the main rodent one (a role for GLUT3 in human beta cells was not found in the full text read, so it is not shown). Glucokinase half-maximal glucose values are not quoted; only its qualitative rate-limiting role is. Step 2 begins with glucokinase and glycolysis, and the signal is the ATP/ADP ratio rather than ATP alone. Step 3 names the channel as Kir6.2 + SUR1. Step 4 shows L-type and P/Q-type channels. Step 5 shows docked granules fusing through SNARE proteins and insulin crossing the thin capillary wall into the blood.

Simplified. Sizes, positions and speeds are illustrative and time is compressed. Channels and transporters are drawn on one face of the cell for clarity; insulin granule exocytosis is targeted towards the capillaries. The K-ATP drawing is a schematic with two Kir6.2 and two SUR1 (the real channel is an octamer, 4 + 4 subunits). Glucose is drawn arriving from the same capillary that takes insulin away. Left out: T-type channels, other K⁺ channels, amplifying (K-ATP-independent) pathways, incretins, the Golgi and ER, and neighbouring cells. Some statements are rodent-specific and are marked as such in the hover text.
